title: Five years: the practices
hook: seva, kirtan, langar, simran and the gurdwara
tomorrow: one bus ride, seven prayers. which line from each does Simran keep?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stories: sakhis told for their point, and the one Simran picked, Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana on the road. So she invited Maya to the gurdwara before the send-off.

Her shoes. That's the first thing Maya notices: a wall of shoes at the door, sneakers next to work boots next to tiny sandals. Then the scarf Simran hands her for her hair. Then the hall downstairs, people sitting in long rows on the floor, a volunteer coming down the line with a pitcher of water. Nobody asks Maya who she is. Somebody just puts a plate in front of her. On the drive home she has one question. Why do they feed anybody who walks in?
screen: `A WALL OF SHOES.` → `ROWS ON THE FLOOR.` → `WHY FEED ANYBODY WHO WALKS IN?`

segments.voice: Simran's answer is the whole list of practices, because they hold each other up. Seva, service with no pay, is who cooked the dal and who'll wash the pots. Kirtan is the hymns being sung upstairs. Simran, the practice her name comes from, is the Name kept in mind while the hands work. The gurdwara is the door that opens on all of it. And langar is the meal, but the point is the row. Everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food, whoever they are. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the langar before they came to see him, and that even an emperor sat in the row. Here's where a neighbor tradition says something close. In the Letter to the Hebrews, Christians read: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Both say the stranger at the door gets fed. That's the shared ground. And an honest difference: the Hebrews line gives a reason in the guest, some guests have been angels. Langar puts its reason in the seating. Nobody is higher on the floor than anybody else. Maya thinks about it at a red light. Then she says the dal was really good, and could she come back.
screen: `SEVA, KIRTAN, SIMRAN, THE GURDWARA.` · `THE POINT IS THE ROW.` · `ENTERTAINED ANGELS UNAWARES.` · `ONE REASON IN THE GUEST, ONE IN THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `THE PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: Choose the one practice you've actually kept: a line of kirtan hummed, Waheguru on the breath, or a small act of service you can do right where you are. Do two unhurried minutes of it now, small and real.
Five years: the practices. Seva, kirtan, langar, simran and the gurdwara, each one holding up the others.
Keep this one: the practices, and a row on the floor where nobody sits higher. Maya wants to come back.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen run by volunteers, where anyone may eat; guests remove their shoes and cover their heads, and the meal is usually eaten sitting in rows on the floor.

fork.reveal: langar's point is the seating: whoever you are, you sit on the same floor and eat the same food. free food alone isn't the whole idea.

chat.meaning: In langar everyone sits in the same rows and eats the same food, whoever they are. The seating is the teaching.

langar.meaning: the gurdwara's free kitchen and shared meal

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape wisdom. One question ('why do they feed anybody who walks in?'), the Sikh answer (the practices, and langar's row), then the unity thread: a neighbor tradition in its own words (Hebrews 13:2, KJV) and one honest difference (Hebrews grounds hospitality in the guest, who may be an angel; langar grounds it in equal seating). No ranking; never 'all the same'.
